Pashur
păsh'ūr
n. (the priest and temple governor who beat Jeremiah and put him in the stocks — renamed by the prophet Magor-missabib, Terror on every side)
From Hebrew Pashchur, of uncertain meaning; a splitting or a freedom has been proposed, and an Egyptian derivation “portion of Horus” is possible. Whatever it meant, Jeremiah replaced it with one that could not be mistaken.

Biblical Definition

Pashur the son of Immer was a priest and “chief governor in the house of the LORD” (Jer 20:1) — the temple's chief officer of order, responsible for keeping the peace in its courts. He kept it in the usual way: “Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD” (Jer 20:2). A prophet flogged and pilloried overnight, by the man whose office was the sanctity of the sanctuary, at its own gate. In the morning Pashur let him out, and Jeremiah gave him a new name: “The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib” (Jer 20:3) — Terror round about — and a sentence: “thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies” (Jer 20:6). It is out of that night in the stocks that the darkest of the prophet's confessions comes, the passage that begins “O LORD, thou hast deceived me” and ends with the fire shut up in his bones. A different Pashur, son of Melchiah, later carries Zedekiah's enquiry to Jeremiah and joins those who cast him into the miry dungeon.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Pashur; in sacred history he is the priest and governor of the temple who smote Jeremiah and set him in the stocks.

expand to see more

PASHUR, n. The son of Immer, a priest and chief governor in the house of the Lord in the days of Jehoiakim.

He smote Jeremiah and put him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin.

Jeremiah on the morrow called his name Magormissabib, that is, terror round about.

He was foretold that he should go captive to Babylon and die there with all his friends.

Another Pashur, the son of Melchiah, was sent by Zedekiah to enquire of the Lord by Jeremiah.

Key Scripture

Jer 20:1 — "Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the LORD, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things."

Jer 20:2 — "Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD."

Jer 20:3 — "And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then said Jeremiah unto him, The LORD hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magormissabib."

Jer 20:6 — "And thou, Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house shall go into captivity: and thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies."

Modern Corruption

Persecution is imagined as coming from outside the church; Jeremiah's stocks stood at the temple gate and were ordered by the temple's own officer.

expand to see more

Pashur is the reminder that the sharpest opposition to the word of God has usually come from inside the religious establishment. He was not a Babylonian; he was a priest, of the course of Immer, holding a real office in the real temple of the true God, and he had the whip out because a preacher had said the city would fall. The pattern runs through Scripture — the prophets stoned in the courts, the Lord Jesus delivered up by the chief priests, Stephen killed by the council, Paul's worst dangers “in perils among false brethren” (2Co 11:26). A church can build a whole apparatus of order whose practical function is to keep unwelcome truth out of its own courts, and the men who run it will believe they are defending holiness.

The second thing is the renaming, because it shows how God answers this. Jeremiah does not fight back and does not appeal; he pronounces a name. Magor-missabib, terror on every side, is a phrase Jeremiah uses of the coming invasion, and now it is fastened to the man who thought himself the guardian of safety. The one who put the prophet in stocks to stop the word about Babylon will himself die in Babylon. And Jer 20:7-9, written the same morning, keeps the account honest about the cost: the prophet accuses God of overpowering him, resolves to speak no more in His name, and finds the word “as a burning fire shut up in my bones” that he could not stay. Faithfulness in that chapter is not serenity; it is being unable to stop.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Pashchur (H6583), Pashur; Magor mis-Sabib (H4036), terror round about; mahpeketh (H4115), the stocks.

expand to see more

Hebrew Pashchur (H6583) — Pashur; borne by several priests, two of them opponents of Jeremiah.

Hebrew Magor mis-Sabib (H4036) — Magormissabib, “terror on every side”; Jeremiah's renaming of him.

Hebrew mahpeketh (H4115) — the stocks; from haphak, to overturn, because the body was twisted in them.

Hebrew paqid nagid — chief governor, overseer; the temple police office Pashur held (Jer 20:1).

Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — a lie; “to whom thou hast prophesied lies” (Jer 20:6).

Usage

"“Chief governor in the house of the LORD” — the office that ordered the beating."

"“Put him in the stocks… by the house of the LORD” — persecution at the sanctuary gate."

"“Not… Pashur, but Magormissabib” — a name the prophet gave and God kept."
